# About

URL: https://kompositenews.com/about/

About Komposite News
Komposite News is an independent digital publication covering artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital assets, enterprise technology, cybersecurity, fintech and capital markets. We write for executives, founders, investors, developers and policy professionals who need to understand how technology and finance are changing each other.
Our coverage prioritizes reporting and analysis over hype. We are interested in what is being built, what it costs, who is buying it and what the consequences are, and we hold breathless claims from any direction to the same standard of evidence.
Ownership and funding: Komposite News is independently operated. Any commercial relationship relevant to a story is disclosed within that story, and sponsored content is always clearly labeled. Questions about the publication can be directed through our contact page.

# Editorial Standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/editorial-standards/

Editorial Standards
Komposite News reports facts we can verify and clearly distinguishes reporting from analysis and opinion. News stories describe what happened. Pieces labeled Analysis interpret events and draw conclusions from evidence. Pieces labeled Opinion argue a point of view and represent their author.
We attribute information to sources wherever possible, grant anonymity only when information is significant and cannot otherwise be obtained, and independently verify claims before publishing them. We do not accept payment for editorial coverage, and staff may not trade on non-public information obtained through reporting.
Sponsored or partner content, when it appears, is labeled unambiguously and is never presented in editorial form without that label. Errors, when they occur, are corrected promptly and transparently under our corrections policy.

Corrections
When Komposite News publishes an error of fact, we correct it as quickly as possible. Corrected articles carry a note describing what was wrong and when it was fixed. Significant corrections are logged on this page.
To request a correction, contact the newsroom via our contact page with the article link and the specific claim at issue. We review every request.
No corrections have been logged for the current publication period.

# AI Policy

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai-policy/

AI Policy
Komposite News uses artificial intelligence as a production tool, not as a replacement for editorial judgment. AI systems may assist with research organization, copy editing, translation, and site infrastructure. Every published story is reviewed and approved by a human editor before publication, and responsibility for accuracy rests with the newsroom, not with any tool used to produce it.
We do not publish AI-generated statements attributed to real people, AI-fabricated data, or synthetic imagery presented as photography. Illustrations are labeled as illustrations, photographs carry credits and licenses, and sample or demonstration data is labeled as such wherever it appears.
This policy will evolve with the technology. Questions about how a specific story was produced can be directed to the newsroom via our contact page.

# What buyers actually do with an SBOM

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/sbom-what-buyers-do-with-it/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z

Software bills of materials are now routinely produced and routinely ignored, and the gap between generating one and acting on it is where the risk sits.

The argument about whether vendors should produce a software bill of materials is over. Vendors produce them. The interesting question, and the one procurement teams are least prepared for, is what happens to the file after it arrives.
An SBOM is an inventory: the components inside a piece of software, their versions, and their relationships to one another. Its value is entirely conditional. It answers one question well, which is whether a newly disclosed vulnerability is present in something already installed, and it answers that question only if somebody is holding it when the disclosure lands.
The baseline moved this year. American authorities published an updated set of minimum elements, replacing guidance that had stood since the original executive order and raising what a compliant document is expected to contain.
That update matters more than it sounds, because the minimum elements are what contracts point at. A purchase order rarely specifies a format in detail. It references a standard, and the standard quietly determines how much work a vendor has to do.
Adoption across the European market has been surveyed rather than assumed. The EU cybersecurity agency's review of where SBOM practice actually stands describes an ecosystem where generation is increasingly routine and consumption remains the weak link.
That asymmetry is the whole story. Producing an SBOM is a build-pipeline problem, and build pipelines are the part of software organizations most amenable to automation. Consuming one is an operations problem, and operations teams are already the most oversubscribed function in most security programs.
The result is a familiar organizational pattern. A file arrives, satisfies a contractual requirement, and is stored where nothing queries it. The obligation is met and the risk is unchanged, which is the worst of both outcomes because it also produces a record showing the buyer was told.
Teams that get value from the practice describe the same prerequisite, and it is not tooling. It is knowing what software they run, at which version, in which environment, well enough to join that list against an inventory. Organizations that cannot answer the first question gain nothing from the second.
Regulatory drivers keep expanding the population who must care. Medical device guidance, the European cyber resilience regime and federal procurement terms each require the artifact in their own context, and each has a different theory of what the recipient is supposed to do with it.
Practitioners are candid that the honest use case is narrower than the marketing. When a widely used component is found to be catastrophically vulnerable, an SBOM turns a week of frantic archaeology into a database query. Between those events it is a maintenance cost.
That is a reasonable trade and a smaller claim than the one usually made for it. The organizations doing this well are not the ones with the best-formatted files. They are the ones who can answer, on the afternoon the disclosure lands, where the affected component is running.

# What an attestation must prove

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/what-an-attestation-must-prove/
Section: Crypto
By: Marcus Oyelaran
Published: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z

Stablecoin law requires monthly examination of reserves, and the open rulemaking question is what level of assurance that examination must actually deliver.

The argument about whether stablecoin issuers should publish their reserves is finished. Federal law requires it. The argument that replaced it is narrower, more technical, and determines whether the requirement means very much: what an examination of those reserves has to establish.
The statute sets the frame. The GENIUS Act requires permitted issuers to publish the composition of their reserves monthly, to have those reports examined by a registered public accounting firm, and to obtain certifications from the chief executive and chief financial officer.
Monthly is a demanding cadence for anything an accounting firm signs. Most public company reporting is quarterly with a single annual audit, so the law is asking for a recurring procedure that has no exact precedent at this frequency.
The open question is the assurance level, and it is not a technicality. An examination performed at limited assurance concludes that nothing came to the practitioner's attention suggesting a problem. One performed at reasonable assurance states positively that the reserves are what the issuer says they are.
Those are different products with different costs and very different meanings to a reader, and the same document title can describe either. A holder comparing two issuers' monthly reports has no reliable way to tell which standard produced them without reading the fine print.
Regulators are consulting rather than assuming. Rulemaking has asked directly whether the examination should be conducted at reasonable assurance, under established attestation standards, or under an alternative framework built for the purpose.
The content of the disclosure is comparatively settled. The expected reporting covers the par value of coins outstanding, the fair value of reserve assets by category, the weighted average maturity of Treasury holdings, the names of custodians and depository institutions, and a reconciliation showing reserves at least equal outstanding coins.
That reconciliation is the heart of it. Everything else describes the portfolio; the reconciliation is the statement that the portfolio covers the liability, and it is the sentence a holder is actually relying on when they treat a token as a dollar.
Supervisors have published implementation requirements through the ordinary rulemaking process, including standards for insured depository institutions and supervised issuers, which is how a novel instrument gets absorbed into an existing supervisory apparatus.
The practical effect of a strong answer would be consolidation. A monthly reasonable-assurance examination is expensive, requires reserve assets an accounting firm can verify quickly, and is easiest for issuers holding short Treasuries at large custodians, which is a narrower field than the one that exists today.
That may be the intended outcome. A payment instrument that circulates as a dollar substitute is a poor place for structural creativity, and the assurance standard is the lever that decides how much of it survives.

# What a seed round now requires

URL: https://kompositenews.com/startups/what-a-seed-round-now-requires/
Section: Startups
By: Grace Lindqvist
Published: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z

Seed rounds now arrive after revenue and retention evidence that once belonged to Series A, and the gap between rounds has stretched past two years.

The seed round kept its name and quietly changed its meaning. What investors now expect before writing that check is roughly what a Series A required a few years ago, and founders planning against the old definition run out of money at the point they expected to raise.
The clearest expression of the shift is time. Data assembled from company cap tables shows the interval between rounds stretching well past two years, which means a seed round is no longer bridging to a nearby milestone. It has to fund the company to a materially different business.
That arithmetic changes how much to raise and what to promise. A round sized for eighteen months against a market that now takes twenty-four produces a company that is technically alive and practically unfundable, holding a deck full of progress and a bank balance that ends the conversation.
Investors describe the bar in terms of evidence rather than vision. Revenue that recurs, retention that survives a renewal cycle, and unit economics the founder can explain without a chart have replaced the narrative rounds that characterized the last cycle.
Pre-seed absorbed the difference. What used to be called seed is now a distinct earlier stage with its own norms and its own investors, which means the ladder gained a rung rather than losing one, and the founder climbs the same distance in more steps.
Formation costs falling has made this possible without making it pleasant. Building a credible product is cheaper than it has ever been, so the evidence investors demand is now genuinely obtainable before a round, which is precisely why it is demanded.
The concentration of capital into a narrow band of companies compounds the effect. When most of a fund's deployment goes to a small number of category-defining bets, the diligence applied to everything else tightens, because those checks have to clear a higher internal bar to justify the attention.
Founders who have raised recently describe the practical adaptation as unglamorous. Charge earlier than feels comfortable, treat the first ten paying customers as the fundraise rather than as a precursor to it, and keep the burn low enough that the round is optional for a quarter longer than planned.
The uncomfortable part is what this selects for. Requiring commercial evidence before capital favors founders who can survive unpaid for longer, which is a filter on personal circumstances as much as on ability, and the industry has not found a good answer to that.
Investors are candid that the discipline is real and its distribution is not. The companies that clear the new bar are unquestionably stronger at the same stage than their predecessors, and some number of good companies never got far enough to be measured.
The stage will keep its name regardless. It is worth understanding that the word now describes a company with customers, and planning the eighteen months before it accordingly.

# AI in the order flow: what machine trading is doing to volatility

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/volatility-market-structure-ai-trading/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z

Adaptive execution and model-driven strategies are changing intraday dynamics in ways researchers are only beginning to measure.

Machine learning has been in markets for years, but the current generation of adaptive execution and model-driven strategies behaves differently from its rule-based ancestors, and researchers are working out what that means for volatility itself.
Early findings are mixed in instructive ways. Adaptive strategies appear to dampen volatility in normal conditions, adjusting quickly to absorb flow imbalances, while contributing to sharper moves when many models respond to the same signal simultaneously. Calm most days, and a faster crowd on the days that matter.
Regulators are asking measurement questions before policy ones: how much flow is model-driven, how correlated are the models, and whether existing circuit breakers match the speed of the herding they are meant to interrupt. Exchanges, holding the data, have become reluctant referees in the debate.
RelatedDigital asset market making becomes an institutional business ›Practitioners mostly shrug at the framing. Every generation of market technology, they note, was accused of breaking volatility until it became the baseline against which the next generation was accused. The honest answer is that the market is running the experiment on itself, and the results publish in real time.

# Machine identity sprawl becomes security's biggest inventory problem

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/identity-machine-workloads/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z

Service accounts, API keys, and agent credentials now outnumber human identities many times over, and governance is racing the growth.

For every human identity in a modern enterprise there are many machine ones, service accounts, API keys, certificates, and now AI agent credentials, and most organizations cannot count them, let alone govern them. Machine identity has become the inventory problem that defines the next phase of identity security.
The risk profile is distinctive: machine credentials are long-lived, widely copied, and rarely owned by anyone who remembers creating them. Incident reviews repeatedly trace breaches to forgotten service accounts with standing privileges, and the remediation is lifecycle discipline, issuance, rotation, expiry, applied at a scale human identity never required.
RelatedCybersecurity spending shifts toward identity and resilience ›Agentic AI raised the stakes by adding credentials that act autonomously. The emerging standard treats every agent as a governed identity with scoped permissions and an accountable human sponsor, which is less a new idea than the old one, finally enforced on the population that grew fastest.

# Enterprises write the rulebook for AI-generated code

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-coding-tools-enterprise-standards/
Section: AI
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z
Updated: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z

Provenance tracking, review gates, and dependency policies are turning AI coding assistance from a developer perk into governed infrastructure.

AI coding assistants arrived in enterprises through developer enthusiasm and settled in ahead of policy. The policy is now catching up. Engineering organizations are formalizing rules for machine-generated code: what must be tracked, what must be reviewed differently, and what may not be generated at all.
Provenance is the anchor requirement. Compliance teams want to know which code a model wrote, which model wrote it, and what the model was shown, both for license exposure and for the audits that regulated industries already face. Tooling vendors have responded with attribution tracking that engineering leaders describe as necessary and nobody describes as finished.
RelatedAI infrastructure spending moves into a new phase ›The practical effect on productivity has been smaller than skeptics predicted. Teams report that governance slowed adoption for a quarter and then became routine, the same arc that source control and code review followed in earlier decades. The tools stayed; the anarchy did not.

# Synthetic data moves from workaround to standard practice

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/synthetic-data-enterprise-training/
Section: AI
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-07-23T11:10:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-23T11:10:00Z

Where privacy rules and data scarcity block model training, generated datasets are filling the gap, and auditors are learning to evaluate them.

Enterprises that cannot use their real data are increasingly training on data that never existed. Synthetic datasets, generated to preserve the statistical shape of sensitive records without exposing any individual, have moved from research curiosity to standard tooling in banking, healthcare, and insurance workflows.
The appeal is regulatory as much as technical. A generated dataset that provably contains no customer records simplifies conversations with privacy officers that real data makes impossible, and vendors now compete on the strength of those proofs rather than just fidelity.
RelatedEnterprise buyers push for clearer AI contract terms ›The open question is quality drift. Models trained on synthetic data inherit the blind spots of whatever generated it, and audit teams are developing tests for the gap between synthetic performance and real-world behavior. The consensus emerging among practitioners is unglamorous: synthetic data works, within limits that must be measured rather than assumed.

# AI evaluation grows from afterthought to budget line

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-evaluation-becomes-budget-line/
Section: AI
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z

Enterprises deploying models at scale are formalizing evaluation the way they once formalized QA, and a vendor category is forming around it.

When AI systems were pilots, evaluation was a spreadsheet. Now that they process claims, answer customers, and draft contracts, companies are treating evaluation as standing infrastructure, with dedicated staff, tooling budgets, and sign-off authority over releases.
The change is driven less by regulation than by incident reports. Organizations that shipped model updates without regression testing describe the same experience: a quiet degradation in some workflow no one was watching, discovered by customers rather than dashboards. Formal evaluation pipelines are the institutional response.
A market is forming to serve the need. Startups sell evaluation harnesses, scored datasets tailored to industries, and monitoring that flags drift in production. Incumbent observability vendors are extending into the category, arguing that model behavior is simply another production signal.
RelatedEnterprise buyers push for clearer AI contract terms ›The maturity marker executives cite is procedural: whether a model change can be blocked. In organizations where evaluation owns a veto, the function is real. Where it produces reports no one must read, it remains a spreadsheet with a bigger budget.

# Power availability becomes the master constraint on computing

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/power-constraints-shape-computing/
Section: Technology
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z

Grid interconnection queues, not chip supply, now set the timeline for new capacity, and the industry is reorganizing around electrons.

Ask data center developers what gates their next project and the answer is no longer silicon. It is the interconnection queue, the multi-year wait for utility approval to draw large amounts of power from grids that were not planned for computing's growth curve.
The constraint is reorganizing the industry's geography and structure. Development migrates to regions with spare generation and faster approvals; operators contract directly for new generation, sometimes co-developing it; and a market has emerged in sites whose chief asset is a signed interconnection agreement.
On-site and adjacent generation has moved from contingency to strategy. Gas turbines as bridge power, long-term contracts anchoring new renewable buildouts, and serious capital behind small modular nuclear all reflect the same conclusion: waiting for the grid is the expensive option.
RelatedLiquid cooling stops being optional in AI data centers ›The policy dimension is unavoidable. Computing's power demand lands on ratepayers, regulators, and climate commitments simultaneously, and jurisdictions are diverging on who pays for the upgrades and who gets priority in the queue. Where those questions get answered favorably is, increasingly, where the next generation of infrastructure gets built.

# Shadow AI becomes the new shadow IT

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/shadow-ai-governance-problem/
Section: Business
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z

Employees are routing work through unsanctioned AI tools faster than policies can name them, and enterprises are choosing between control and visibility.

Every technology wave produces its shadow, and AI's arrived on schedule. Employees across functions are routing drafting, analysis, and coding through personal accounts on consumer AI tools, outside procurement, outside logging, and outside whatever policy the company wrote last quarter.
The governance instinct is prohibition, and the operational evidence is that prohibition fails quietly. Organizations that blocked consumer tools report usage migrating to personal devices, trading visible risk for invisible risk. The emerging alternative is substitution: sanctioned tools good enough that the shadow versions lose their appeal, paired with monitoring that treats AI traffic like any other data flow.
RelatedEnterprise software pricing strains under the weight of AI ›Security leaders describe the moment in familiar terms, because they lived it with cloud storage and messaging apps. The lesson they cite from those episodes is consistent: the workforce adopts what works, and governance succeeds by arriving with a better answer rather than a longer denial.

# Instant payments become table stakes in B2B

URL: https://kompositenews.com/fintech/instant-payments-b2b-standard/
Section: Fintech
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z

Real-time rails are moving from consumer novelty to supplier expectation, and the software layer on top is where the margin lives.

Instant payment rails, built for consumers splitting dinner, are being colonized by business finance. Supplier payments, insurance disbursements, and payroll adjustments increasingly ride real-time systems, and the expectation is spreading through supply chains faster than the infrastructure teams behind it anticipated.
The shift exposes where the value actually sits. Moving money instantly is becoming a commodity; knowing why it moved is not. The software that attaches invoices, remittance data, and reconciliation to real-time payments commands the margin the rails themselves are losing.
Corporate adoption follows a practical script: start with the payments where speed is worth money, urgent supplier releases, claim payouts, final payrolls, then expand as finance teams trust the controls. Fraud tooling has had to accelerate in parallel, since irrevocable and instant is a demanding combination.
RelatedWhen software spends: payments build an authorization layer for AI agents ›Banks find themselves both essential and squeezed, operating the rails while fintech intermediaries own the customer experience above them. The competitive response, embedding payment capabilities directly into the software businesses already use, is reshaping bank product organizations around a fact they long resisted: the interface is the relationship.

# Stablecoin Reserve reporting converges on common standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-standards/
Section: Crypto
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z
Updated: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z

Monthly attestations are giving way to standardized disclosures that let treasurers compare issuers the way they compare money market funds.

Stablecoin issuers are learning to speak the language of money market funds. Reserve disclosures, once a patchwork of voluntary attestations in incompatible formats, are converging on standardized reporting of composition, maturity, and counterparties, driven by regulation in some jurisdictions and competitive pressure everywhere else.
The audience is corporate. Treasurers evaluating stablecoins for payments want the same visibility they get from a fund fact sheet, and issuers courting that demand have discovered that transparency is a product feature. Disclosure quality now appears in payment providers' issuer scorecards alongside redemption terms.
Standardization enables comparison, and comparison disciplines behavior. Analysts publishing side-by-side reserve breakdowns note measurable shifts toward shorter maturities and simpler holdings since standard formats took hold, the market rewarding conservatism it can finally see.
RelatedStablecoin law meets its implementation year ›Gaps remain, particularly in real-time reporting and the treatment of reserves held across borders. But the direction is set, and it points toward stablecoins being evaluated with the tools of cash management rather than the vocabulary of crypto.

# Stablecoin law meets its implementation year

URL: https://kompositenews.com/policy/stablecoin-law-implementation-year/
Section: Policy
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2025-12-04T10:10:00Z
Updated: 2025-12-04T10:10:00Z

With frameworks enacted, the action has moved to licensing queues, reserve examinations, and the fine print of redemption.

The stablecoin statutes are written; the stablecoin industry is now living in their footnotes. Licensing queues, reserve examination schedules, and supervisory guidance on redemption mechanics have become the substance of the policy story, and the firms treating implementation as core competence are pulling ahead of those who treated enactment as the finish line.
The examinations are having their intended disciplining effect. Reserve compositions have simplified, attestations have hardened toward audits, and redemption commitments now carry operational detail, timelines, channels, stress procedures, that marketing language previously blurred.
RelatedAI regulation enters its implementation phase ›The competitive consequence mirrors every regulated industry: compliance capacity is strategy. The licensed issuers describe their examination binders, without irony, as moats, and the market share data increasingly agrees with them.

# Incident reporting clocks start ticking for critical infrastructure

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/critical-infrastructure-reporting-rules/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2025-11-19T10:45:00Z
Updated: 2025-11-19T10:45:00Z

Mandatory disclosure windows are standardizing how fast operators must tell regulators, and readiness has become a drill.

Critical infrastructure operators now measure incident response in regulatory hours. Mandatory reporting windows, seventy-two hours here, thirty-six there, materially sooner for ransom payments, have standardized the clock that starts when an intrusion is discovered, and legal, security, and communications teams are drilling to it.
The operational effect is decision speed. Determining whether an event is reportable requires triage discipline that many organizations lacked, and tabletop exercises now rehearse the classification call as intensively as the containment. Counsel describe the deadline as clarifying: ambiguity that once justified delay now creates exposure.
RelatedSoftware supply chain rules begin to bite ›Regulators promise the aggregated reports will improve collective defense, and early threat advisories citing reported patterns suggest the loop is beginning to function. Operators remain wary of disclosure risk, but the compliance question has moved from whether to report to how fast the machine can decide.

# Interoperability standards take shape for institutional chains

URL: https://kompositenews.com/blockchain/interoperability-standards-institutional-chains/
Section: Blockchain
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z
Updated: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z

Messaging standards bodies and blockchain consortia are converging on formats that let regulated ledgers talk to each other, and to the systems banks already run.

The institutional blockchain world is discovering what payments learned decades ago: networks that cannot interoperate stay small. Standards work, unfashionable and slow, has become the venue where the next phase of adoption is actually being decided.
The convergence underway joins two traditions. Financial messaging bodies bring the discipline of standardized data formats that banks already parse, while blockchain consortia bring transfer protocols proven on public networks. The emerging designs let a tokenized asset move between regulated ledgers while carrying the structured information compliance systems require.
Progress is measured in pilots that would once have been impossible: assets issued on one institution's ledger settling against payment on another's, with both sides reconciled automatically. Participants emphasize that none of it required the institutions to share a chain, only a vocabulary.
RelatedBanks test blockchain settlement without abandoning existing rails ›The stakes are consolidation versus fragmentation. If common standards hold, tokenized markets can scale across institutions the way correspondent banking did. If they fail, each network remains an island, and the efficiency case for the technology weakens accordingly.

# The secondary market becomes startups' pressure valve

URL: https://kompositenews.com/startups/secondaries-startup-liquidity/
Section: Startups
By: Grace Lindqvist
Published: 2026-06-04T11:30:00Z
Updated: 2026-06-04T11:30:00Z

Structured tenders for employees and early investors are normalizing partial liquidity, changing when companies must exit at all.

The decade-long path to liquidity broke something in startup employment, and the secondary market has become the repair. Structured tender offers, company-sanctioned windows where employees and early holders sell to institutional buyers, have moved from rarity to expected milestone at growth-stage companies.
The normalization changed incentives across the table. Employees can realize value without leaving; early funds can return capital without forcing exits; and companies can stay private on their own schedule rather than their shareholders'. Late-stage investors describe tender allocations as a standard entry path into oversubscribed names.
RelatedVenture funding returns to infrastructure software ›The discipline questions have answers now too: information rules, price discovery through auction rather than negotiation, and caps that keep selling from signaling. What was once a whispered accommodation has acquired paperwork, which in financial markets is what maturity looks like.

# The SEC's examiners put super intelligence on the 2027 list

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/the-sec-examiners-put-super-intelligence-on-the-2027-list/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-10-23T15:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-23T15:20:00Z

The SEC's Division of Examinations on Friday set its fiscal 2027 priorities, naming registrants' use of super intelligence, cyber resilience, private credit and tokenisation.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Division of Examinations on Friday published its fiscal year 2027 examination priorities, naming registrants' use of what it calls "super intelligence" (SI), cybersecurity and customer data, private credit and tokenisation among the areas it considers higher risk, the SEC said. The priorities apply across what the release calls "the Division's more than 34,000 registrants".
The priorities document is a staff statement. A disclaimer on its first page says it is not a rule, regulation or statement of the Commission, which has neither approved nor disapproved it, and that it creates no new or additional obligations. The release says the list is not exhaustive and that the division may adjust its focus in response to market events and new developments.
SI appears in the leadership message before the priorities themselves. The division says registrants are "increasingly incorporating super intelligence (SI) into their businesses", using generative tools for research, drafting, coding and client communications, as well as advisory and portfolio management functions and compliance monitoring. It says it is "intensifying its efforts" to understand how the technologies influence outcomes and whether firms continue to comply with existing, technology-neutral obligations. The division adds that it is working to bring SI into its own examinations and risk assessment "without displacing examiner judgment".
The section on emerging financial technology is more specific. It says threat actors are using SI to automate and accelerate cyberattacks, and that examiners will review registrants' preparation for SI-related threats such as SI-generated phishing messages and synthetic or deepfake voice and video used for social engineering. The division will also prioritise policies for monitoring SI used in fraud prevention and detection, back-office operations, anti-money-laundering and Regulation Best Interest compliance, and trading. For automated investment tools, it will test whether representations are fair and accurate, whether operations and controls match what investors were told, and whether algorithms produce advice consistent with investors' investment profiles or stated strategies.
Cybersecurity and operational resilience remain a priority, with examiners reviewing governance, data loss prevention, access controls, and response and recovery protocols, including for ransomware. The division says it will assess the risks of registrants' increased use of third-party service providers and shared technologies. Under the amended Regulation S-P, staff will evaluate incident-response policies, customer notification procedures and oversight of service providers. For investment advisers, the document also flags firms that use third parties to access clients' accounts, where existing controls "may be insufficient to protect client assets and data".
On products, the division says it will prioritise advisers that recommend investments that are difficult to trade, have unusual features or are illiquid. Its examples include loans provided by private funds or business development companies, stakes in private companies held through special purpose vehicles, and higher-risk products such as exchange-traded funds based on less liquid assets, option-based funds, inverse and single-stock ETFs, and zero-days-to-expiration options. For private fund advisers, examiners will check disclosures on debt, fund-level lines of credit, affiliated service providers and the accuracy of fee and expense calculations.
Market infrastructure gets its own entries. Examinations of clearing agencies will focus on areas including risk management of defaults, recovery and wind-down, securities lending, operations and tokenisation, and on compliance with new rules including those on expanded Treasury clearing. Under Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity, examiners will look at emerging trends including SI, tokenisation of securities, extended trading hours and quantum computing. The document does not mention crypto assets; tokenisation is the nearest it comes.
Paul S. Atkins, the SEC's chairman, said in the release: "Examinations are one of the Commission's most important tools for promoting compliance with the federal securities laws." Keith Cassidy, the division's director, said: "The markets we oversee continue to evolve rapidly, and the examination program must evolve with them." The document says a central focus this year is strengthening how registrants get access to the observations examiners gather, and it notes an enhanced memorandum of understanding with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission that deepens coordination between the two agencies.
Why it matters: the priorities are not rules, but they tell regulated firms where examiners will ask questions in the coming year. For firms that have put generative tools into research, client communications or compliance, the document signals that disclosures, controls and monitoring around those tools will be examined under existing law. It also arrives as the SEC works on other plans for funds, including the cross-trading proposal Komposite covered this month, and as incidents such as Railway's key-rotation warning keep third-party risk in view.

# Quest says patient records were reached through its ordering portal

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/quest-says-patient-records-were-reached-through-its-ordering-portal/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-10-23T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-23T15:00:00Z

Quest Diagnostics said in an SEC filing that an unauthorised party accessed patient records in its Quanum LSM ordering system; it has not said how many people are affected.

Quest Diagnostics, the US laboratory-testing company, said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission dated Thursday that it learned on Wednesday of unauthorised access to its Quanum LSM system and believes an unauthorised party accessed certain patient records. The filing does not say how many patients are affected.
The 8-K describes Quanum LSM as a system "which certain clients use to place test orders, receive and look up results". Quest said it started its incident-response procedures to contain the activity, notified federal law enforcement and engaged outside cybersecurity experts. The full scope remains under investigation, the filing says, and the incident has not materially disrupted the company's operations or its ability to serve patients.
A notice on Quest's website, marked as of 08:00 Eastern on Friday, says the company paused access to Quanum Lab Services Manager on discovering the incident. Providers that order through direct laboratory-system interfaces or electronic medical records can carry on, and Quanum LSM customers can use paper requisitions or Quanum eLabs in the meantime. The notice says Quest anticipated restoring full service "as soon as" 23 October. Two other products, Essential Insights and LabHQ, were paused as a precaution; Quest says no data was accessed in them. It says it believes "some patient data within Quanum LSM was accessed" and is working to determine which data, and that the incident is not related to this week's PHP programming-language flaws.
Quest says it will notify affected patients, providers and health plans as the law requires, and that letters to patients will describe the resources available, including credit and identity monitoring. TechCrunch reported that Quest did not say when the intrusion began or whether attackers have demanded payment, and that a spokesperson, Amanda Rivera, did not answer its questions and pointed to the notice. TechCrunch also noted that the notice page carries code telling search engines not to list it.
It is not Quest's first exposure of patient data. In June 2019 the company disclosed that a breach at American Medical Collection Agency, a billing collections vendor, had reached information on about 11.9 million Quest patients; it said then that laboratory results were not affected. This time the system involved is Quest's own.
TechCrunch placed the incident in a run of healthcare attacks this year, including those at Stryker, Boston Scientific, CareCloud, Craneware and McKesson.
Why it matters: a laboratory ordering portal holds names, test orders and results for many practices at once, so one point of access can reach many providers' patients. So far the 8-K is the only source with a firm date and the company's own scope language. Komposite has reported on similar single-vendor exposure in the ConnectWise intrusions and Railway's call to rotate keys.

# a16z drops 'crypto' from the name of its crypto unit

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/a16z-drops-crypto-from-the-name-of-its-crypto-unit/
Section: Crypto
By: Marcus Oyelaran
Published: 2026-10-23T14:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-23T14:40:00Z

Andreessen Horowitz renamed a16z Crypto as a16z Frontier, widening its new fund beyond crypto start-ups to frontier technology while saying it will keep investing in crypto.

Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) has renamed its digital-asset unit from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier and is widening the scope of its new fund beyond crypto start-ups, according to an announcement signed by Chris Dixon, the unit's managing partner. TechCrunch reported that the firm announced the change on Thursday.
"We're renaming a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier," the post says. It describes the change as "an expansion" towards "frontier startups", which it defines as companies building new technologies and creating markets that may take years to develop, and says the firm "will continue to invest in crypto and related ventures and advocate for sensible crypto regulation". Mr Dixon argues that as blockchains have become more widely used the label matters less, and that it makes more sense to define companies by what they do than by the technology they use.
The new focus is the current wave of AI. The post names brand-new uses of AI rather than faster versions of old tasks, a proliferation of new devices including autonomous machines that can act in the physical world, advances in biology and medicine, and networks built for machines and AI agents rather than people. It says blockchains will play "a significant role" in that, through stablecoins, programmable financial services and machine-to-machine transactions. Mr Dixon writes that he will lead the fund with the firm's founders, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and general partners Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet, and that operating teams will keep supporting existing and future portfolio companies. The post gives no fund size or date.
TechCrunch said the unit has raised nearly $10bn across five funds since it launched in 2018, and backed Coinbase among other companies; Komposite has not verified those figures. The outlet framed the rename as "a sign that crypto and blockchain-focused investing has receded in importance", and said a16z and rival firms had struggled for years to push crypto's usefulness beyond financial rails, trading applications and speculative assets. That is TechCrunch's reading; a16z's post presents the change as a widening of scope, not a retreat.
TechCrunch also reported, citing The Information, that Ali Yahya, who joined the crypto strategy as its first investor in 2017, has left the firm. Komposite has not confirmed his departure with a16z; he is not among the leaders named in Mr Dixon's post.
Why it matters: a16z is one of the largest backers of digital-asset start-ups, so the name over its door is a signal to founders deciding whom to approach. A rename does not change existing holdings, and the post does not say how the new fund's capital will be split between crypto and everything else. The policy backdrop is in our report on the Senate's stalled market-structure bill, and the AI money flowing elsewhere in Tenstorrent's doubled valuation.

# AI agents tried 2,250 tenants through one backup vendor

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/microsoft-says-agents-hit-2250-tenants-through-connectwise/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-10-22T18:30:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-22T18:30:00Z

Microsoft said China state-aligned Storm-0940 used the ARTEX AI agent framework after compromising ConnectWise Cloud Backup to try sign-ins at over 2,250 tenants.

A China state-aligned group used AI agents to try to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customer tenants after compromising ConnectWise's Cloud Backup service, Microsoft said on Wednesday. It put the pace at 2,900 sign-in attempts a minute.
Microsoft tracks the group as Storm-0940 and says it has been active since 2021, stealing data from organisations in many industries. It assessed that the group was behind the ConnectWise compromise. ConnectWise, which sells IT management software mainly to managed service providers, has suspended Cloud Backup, a service formerly called SkyKick that copies customers' Microsoft 365 data. A tenant is one organisation's own Microsoft 365 environment.
The route in was the trust customers had already given the vendor. After taking control of the identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications, Microsoft said, the attackers' agents used those app credentials to authenticate to customer environments, with no interactive user sign-in needed. In some tenants they went further, into reconnaissance through Microsoft Graph, changes to application credentials that can act as a backdoor, and changes to identities, groups and privileged roles. Microsoft said it found "multiple customer environments" with such follow-on activity, but cautioned that an affected application, or even a successful sign-in, "does not necessarily indicate" that data was accessed or taken. TechCrunch reported that the credentials could let the hackers reach emails and other files.
The tool was ARTEX, which Microsoft describes as an open-source penetration-testing framework of AI agents that can use any AI model and run an attack from reconnaissance to data theft with little human input. Storm-0940 has used it since at least September against organisations in sectors from aerospace and defence to think tanks, Microsoft said, in several cases reaching privileged cloud access less than three hours after first targeting. Microsoft also noted public reporting this month that ARTEX was used in data breaches at Korean financial institutions. Agents "are not constrained by factors affecting humans", it wrote: they work around the clock and try several paths at once.
Not everything worked. Between 10 and 14 October, Microsoft said, infrastructure linked to the group ran an automated password-spray campaign against 327 accounts at eight organisations, logging more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, over 111,000 of them on a single day. Lockouts made up nearly 98 per cent of the activity, and Microsoft saw no successful authentication. ConnectWise's own advisory says it discovered the intrusion on 14 October and first published a notice on Friday 16 October. On 17 October it shut off Cloud Backup access, disabled seven ConnectWise application identities and revoked the certificates used by the affected connections; by 18 October it had also suspended two linked products, SaaS Security and Cloud Management. It reset all accounts and credentials in the affected environment on 19 October and began a phased restoration on Wednesday, which it expects to take several days.
In its update on Thursday, ConnectWise said: "Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise." It added that it has "no indication that other ConnectWise products, services or offerings are impacted by this incident". It has said its systems cannot show whether individual customers' Microsoft 365 tenants were affected, so each must be reviewed. Those are the company's statements, and Komposite has not independently verified them.
Microsoft's advice is specific: keep the affected ConnectWise connections disabled until ConnectWise issues formal restoration instructions, and do not delete the enterprise applications as a first response, so that evidence survives. It told customers to search every tenant for the applications by ID rather than display name, and to review service-principal sign-ins, the log of app-only logins, from at least 15 October, or from 1 October where records allow.
Why it matters: the entry route, a vendor's stored credentials, is familiar; the speed is not. Microsoft's figures describe an automated sweep across thousands of tenants that left defenders little time to respond, even though most of the targeting failed. As we reported, shared vendors concentrate this kind of risk, and Railway's warning on Wednesday that every customer should rotate its keys is another case of one platform holding many companies' secrets.

# The collar can find the dog. Cinnante Canine trains it

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/the-collar-can-find-the-dog-not-train-it/
Section: Technology
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-10-22T18:10:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-22T18:10:00Z

Fi, Halo and Tractive sell GPS dog collars with health tracking and virtual fences; Cinnante Canine argues expert in-house trainers, not gadgets, produce results.

A dog collar in 2026 can report its location over a cellular network, draw a virtual fence and flag unusual scratching, but it cannot teach a recall, according to the makers' own pages. Fi, Halo and Tractive sell GPS trackers on subscription. Cinnante Canine, a Los Angeles-area training company, offers what the hardware cannot: experienced trainers. Its board-and-train programme comes in two tiers, one led by its founder, Joe Cinnante, and one led by his team, the company's site says.
The hardware is specific. Halo, which sells GPS fence collars, lists its Halo Collar 5 at $524, down from $599, on its home page. It claims GPS accuracy of "under 2ft", unlimited virtual fences stored on the collar so they work without signal, and up to 48 hours of battery. A Pack Membership, which Halo says is required to activate GPS, cellular service and fences, starts at $9.99 a month. Fi, whose collar is the Series 3+, claims "up to 3 months" of battery on its site and says every membership includes the collar itself. Fi's pages did not show a price when Komposite read them. Tractive lists its DOG 6 at $79 with up to two weeks of battery, and says it works in "175+ countries" over 2G or LTE networks.
The subscription is where the cost sits. Tractive's plans page starts at $108 billed annually, and lists 365-day location history and heart and respiratory rate monitoring under its Premium tier, against 24 hours of history for Basic users. By our arithmetic, a Halo Collar 5 on its entry plan costs about $644 in its first year, and a Tractive DOG 6 on the cheapest annual plan costs $187. Both figures are before any discount for multi-year terms. The makers' prices are their own, and Komposite did not test the devices.
Health tracking is the newer pitch, and the makers hedge it. Fi says its collar tracks rest, eating, drinking, scratching, licking and barking, and that its AI can catch early signs of "allergies or discomfort". Tractive offers "daily health insights like vitals, activity and sleep", plus bark monitoring that it says can "detect signs of separation anxiety". Its own footnote says: "Tractive is not a medical device." None of the three companies claims its collar diagnoses illness. They describe changes in behaviour that an owner, or a vet, is then expected to interpret.
Training is where the devices meet the argument. Halo's collar can deliver sound, vibration and what it calls "optional static levels", described on its feedback page as a "gentle tap on the shoulder". Halo says "Static is never required" and that "Halo Collar is not a shock collar", distinguishing its feedback from "a single high-voltage electric pulse" in traditional devices. Its boundary training programme was "Developed with Cesar Millan". Halo's own FAQ says the owner, not the collar, should do the training. Those are Halo's descriptions and were not independently verified.
Hand-held remote training collars, or e-collars, divide professional bodies. The American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior (AVSAB) says, in its 2021 position statement as published on its site, that "There is no evidence that aversive methods are more effective than reward-based methods in any context", and lists electronic shock collars among aversive tools. The Certification Council for Professional Dog Trainers (CCPDT), which certifies trainers, takes a different line. Its position statement says it "does not forbid the use of electronic collars" used within its "Humane Hierarchy", but that a certificant "should never" use electric stimulation "as an initial training option".
The most-cited research comes from the University of Lincoln. In a 2020 paper in Frontiers in Veterinary Science, Lucy China, Daniel Mills and Jonathan Cooper compared 63 dogs with recall and chasing problems across three groups of 21. Dogs trained by reward-focused trainers responded better to "Sit" and "Come" after a single command than dogs trained with active e-collars, and the authors found "no evidence to indicate that E-collar training is necessary". They also noted limits: the video came from a 2010-11 government project, groups trained in different seasons, and methods differed beyond the collar itself.
The law is unsettled even where it has moved. Michael Gove, then Environment Secretary, announced in August 2018 that remote-controlled e-collars for dogs and cats would be banned in England, while exempting invisible fences. Draft regulations set a start date of 1 February 2024, and Parliament's Petitions Committee, rejecting a petition in March 2025, said they "came into effect on February 1, 2024". The official register does not show that. legislation.gov.uk still lists the Animal Welfare (Electronic Collars) (England) Regulations 2023 as draft legislation that "has not yet been made as a UK Statutory Instrument". The Royal Kennel Club, which supports a total ban, says the use and sale of shock collars "is currently not prohibited in England". Wales has banned them since 2010.
That is the gap Joe Cinnante has built his business around. A trainer with more than 25 years of experience, he has trained and provided dogs for military and police K9 units, founded Advanced Canine Systems in 2013 and launched Cinnante Canine in 2023, according to his About page. The company's promise is two words: "Real Results." It is pitched at owners who have already paid for something that did not work. "Every day, dog owners invest thousands into training programs that fail to deliver," Cinnante said in a statement to Komposite News.
The model is people rather than hardware. "At Cinnante Canine, your dog's training is never outsourced. Every dog is trained in-house by our team of experts," Cinnante said. The direction is upmarket. The company already works for "a number of very high net worth clients", he said, adding: "Basically what we want to move towards is high end / high level care for affluent clients and their dogs."
Cinnante uses technology where it helps owners follow the work. During a retreat, the company says on its website, "We provide regular updates on your dog's progress, including photos and videos." Its training page offers one-on-one virtual sessions alongside private lessons around Los Angeles, and an online programme with training videos and live Q&A is listed as "COMING SOON!".
The spending is real. The American Pet Products Association puts actual US spending on pets at $158 billion in its latest figures and projects $165 billion for 2026, with training counted inside a $14.3bn "Other Services" line that also covers boarding, grooming, insurance and pet sitting. The collar answers where the dog is, and a growing share of the time how it is. Whether it comes when called is still, on the makers' own account and on Cinnante's, a matter of training. His summary of what owners are paying for is four short sentences: "Better behavior. More trust. More freedom. Less stress."
Komposite has covered the wider shift of AI into consumer hardware, including on-device inference, and the push into connected homes in Apple's front door, built by LG.

# A second Meta share, without the vote

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/a-second-meta-share-without-the-vote/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-10-22T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-22T14:00:00Z

Meta will issue one non-voting Class C share per share held from 19 January 2027, filings show, letting it raise equity without diluting Mark Zuckerberg's control.

Meta Platforms will give shareholders one non-voting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they hold once its new charter takes effect on 19 January 2027, an 8-K filing shows. The company said the stock can be used to raise capital, pay employees and fund acquisitions without diluting anyone's vote.
The board approved the restated charter on Monday 19 October on the unanimous recommendation of a special committee of disinterested and independent directors, the filing says. The next day, seven holding entities linked to Mark Zuckerberg (CZI Holdings and six Chan Zuckerberg Holdings companies), which together held 56.1 per cent of the voting power, approved it by written consent, according to Meta's preliminary information statement. Record and payment dates for the share dividend will be set later; payment is due no later than the fifth business day after the charter takes effect. Meta expects the Class A price to reflect a two-for-one split once the dividend is paid, and intends to list the Class C shares on Nasdaq.
By our arithmetic, the dividend would create about 2.56bn Class C shares. Meta's quarterly report shows 2,214,472,367 Class A and 341,768,886 Class B shares outstanding on 16 October, which sum to 2,556,241,253, assuming no change before the record date.
The point is control. As of 1 October, Mr Zuckerberg, Meta's founder, chairman and chief executive, beneficially owned 1,220,703 Class A and 341,215,148 Class B shares, about 60.6 per cent of total voting power and about 13.4 per cent of the economic interest, the information statement says. The special committee noted he "is not on the verge of losing voting control". It also recorded that he "would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power", and that its adviser, Moelis, estimated Meta could raise at most about $700bn in equity over several years under the current structure before his voting power fell below 50 per cent.
The more unusual terms sit in a Founder Alignment Agreement signed on 20 October. Twenty per cent of the Class C shares Mr Zuckerberg and his permitted transferees receive will be freely saleable, which the information statement says represents 10 per cent of his overall economic stake. The other 80 per cent are "Stapled Class C Shares": for each one sold, he must within two business days sell a Class A or Class B share, convert a Class B share to Class A, or apply credits from earlier sales. A sale that breaks the rule is treated as an automatic conversion of Class B shares into Class A, which carry one vote rather than ten.
The staple loosens on a schedule. At the end of each calendar quarter in which he stays on the executive team or as executive chair full time, 2.5 per cent of his dividend shares are released; after the 32nd such quarter, the rest go. By our arithmetic, 32 quarters at 2.5 per cent is the full 80 per cent, so eight years of qualifying service unstaples everything. He has also committed, for eight years and absent "material unforeseen circumstances", to live in California or wherever Meta has its headquarters.
The filing is plain about why. If California's Proposition 40, a one-time wealth tax on the 3 November ballot, becomes law, Mr Zuckerberg "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion dollar tax payment", and he told the committee he was evaluating moving his primary residence out of California, the information statement says. The freely saleable shares let him pay "his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control". In a July conversation with the lead independent director, he said that paying the tax by selling Class B shares could cut his voting interest to about 53 per cent.
Further one-for-one Class C dividends follow "Doubling Events", when the 30-day volume-weighted Class C price reaches two, four, eight times and so on the $580.60 Class A price of 10 September, provided the compound annual shareholder return since then is at least 10 per cent. In a merger or tender offer, Mr Zuckerberg and his holder group may not take more, or different, consideration than other holders of the same class. After the dividend, if Meta buys back Class A shares, it must use best efforts to buy back at least as many Class C shares.
Meta, quarter to 30 September20262025
Revenue$64,601m$51,242m
Costs and expenses$51,613m$30,707m
Income from operations$12,988m$20,535m
Operating margin20%40%
Net income$9,860m$2,709m
Diluted EPS$3.83$1.05
Source: Meta's third-quarter release, Exhibit 99.1 to its Form 8-K filed 21 October 2026. Unaudited; the company's own figures. 2026 costs include a $9.89bn legal charge.
The plan came with the third-quarter results. Revenue rose 26 per cent to $64.60bn while costs and expenses rose 68 per cent to $51.61bn, including a $9.89bn charge for an August agreement with 52 attorneys general over teen mental health, according to Meta's results release. Capital expenditure, including finance lease principal, was $34.91bn in the quarter, free cash flow was negative $2.12bn, and Meta guided full-year capital expenditure to $135bn-$145bn.
Susan Li, the chief financial officer, told analysts on Wednesday's call: "We believe this share class will maintain our founder led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we are seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI. We do not have any specific financing plans to announce at this time," according to a transcript of the call. Analysts want the shares out quickly. "The sooner the better in our view as it would remove the overhang," Doug Anmuth, an analyst at JPMorgan, said, Yahoo Finance reported; Meta shares fell 2 per cent in premarket trading on Thursday, it said.
There is also a large legal bill. On 25 September a New Mexico jury found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of the state's Unfair Practices Act in a case brought by the state attorney general, and on Wednesday the court imposed a civil penalty of $25bn with 15 per cent post-judgment interest, the company's 10-Q says. Meta says it has accrued an amount for the matter, intends to appeal and may need to post a bond. Raúl Torrez, New Mexico's attorney general, said: "We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," TechCrunch reported, while C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the ruling "makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico".
Why it matters: Meta has so far paid for its AI build-out from operating cash and debt, and with free cash flow now negative it has created a third route, a tradable equity that costs Mr Zuckerberg no votes. Outside shareholders take all the economic dilution from future issuance, and the stapling terms are what they get in return. Komposite has followed the same funding race in OpenAI's search for $30bn and in the SpaceX and Tesla merger talks.

# Twice the capex, less than half the operating profit

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/teslas-operating-margin-halves-as-capital-spending-doubles/
Section: Business
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-10-22T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-22T13:40:00Z

Tesla's third-quarter operating income fell to $718m on flat $28.05bn revenue as capital spending reached $4.73bn and Optimus robot production began in Fremont.

Tesla's third-quarter operating income fell 56 per cent to $718m while its capital spending more than doubled to $4.73bn, according to its quarterly update filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday. Revenue was flat at $28.05bn, and net income attributable to shareholders fell to $787m from $1.37bn.
Revenue was $28,046m against $28,095m a year earlier, down 0.2 per cent by our arithmetic. Gross profit rose to $5,494m, a GAAP gross margin of about 19.6 per cent against 18.0 per cent, so the squeeze came lower down: operating expenses rose 39 per cent to $4,776m by our arithmetic. The operating margin was about 2.6 per cent against 5.8 per cent, a fall of 322 basis points by the company's count. Non-GAAP net income was $1,697m.

Capital expenditure was $4,732m against $2,248m, or 2.1 times by our arithmetic, though below the $5,789m of the second quarter. Operating cash flow was $6,263m and free cash flow $1,531m, and cash and short-term investments rose to $45,447m. On the call, chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said Tesla was "revising our CapEx guidance to be approximately $20 billion for the current year", to be funded "primarily from our cash flows from operations", and that it had "secured capacity to borrow up to $30 billion" with no plans to draw on it this year, according to a transcript of the call.
The update explains the revenue mix. Energy generation and storage revenue fell to $2,881m from $3,415m, "partially due to tariff-related customer refunds", Tesla said, and regulatory credit revenue fell to $113m from $417m. Services and other revenue rose to $4,605m from $3,475m, with what the company called record gross profit of $734m. Deliveries fell 2 per cent to 486,532 vehicles while production rose 4 per cent to 464,391.
"Optimus production began in Fremont on our high-volume lines," Tesla said, describing the units as "the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured." On the call, Elon Musk, the chief executive, called it "what I'd call early production" and said the early part of the ramp "has a shallow slope and is somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product." He said it would take "at least a year, maybe a little longer" to reach a rate of 20,000 units a week. TechCrunch reported the target as 20,000 a week by the end of 2027. It is a goal, not an order book.
On autonomy, Tesla said it began giving Robotaxi rides in Cybercabs in Austin on 3 September, and that the service reached nearly two million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the quarter. Active Full Self-Driving (Supervised) customers, a measure that counts upfront purchases and subscriptions for software that still needs a watching driver, rose to 1.74m from 1.04m. Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of AI software, said on the call: "We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the Robotaxi fleet."
Why it matters: Tesla is spending about twice as much on capital projects while earning less than half as much from operations, and its case now rests on robots, robotaxis and compute rather than on car volumes. Tesla says it will not draw on its new $30bn of borrowing capacity this year. The company's numbers are its own. Komposite reported on Wednesday on the special committees weighing a SpaceX and Tesla merger, which Mr Musk cannot attend.

# Two PHP flaws, and no fix but the patch

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/two-critical-php-flaws-have-no-complete-mitigation/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-10-22T13:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-22T13:20:00Z

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical remote code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.2; the project says only updating is a complete fix.

PHP's maintainers on Wednesday released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 to fix two critical flaws that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a web server, according to the project's security advisory. "There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice," each release note says.
The flaws are CVE-2026-109618, remote code execution through out-of-memory corruption, and CVE-2026-109619, remote code execution through stale global state. Both are rated 9.2 under version 4.0 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, according to the project's GitHub advisories and the US National Vulnerability Database. The project gave advance notice on Tuesday, scheduling the release for 14:00 UTC on Wednesday.
In the first flaw, PHP's handling of an out-of-memory error can interrupt a request while internal data is only partly set up, and the clean-up that follows may then treat that invalid data as valid. In the second, the advisory says, state belonging to one request can survive after its memory is freed, and a later request on the same worker may use it before normal initialisation resets it. The advisory names PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed as exposed, and puts the risk highest for mod_php, citing "a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs."
The stop-gaps are partial. For the memory flaw, the project suggests removing PHP's memory limit in a way applications cannot override and lowering request-size limits, including at the web server or proxy. For the stale-state flaw, it suggests disabling session upload progress and restarting every worker, and warns against relying on ini_set() or .user.ini files. These measures "reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe," it says.
Support is uneven. Linux distributions and long-term-support vendors received the patches in advance, the advisory says. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the project, though its security team published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. The 8.2 branch reaches end of life on 31 December 2026.
Among those credited with reporting the bugs is Wiz Research, the research arm of the cloud security company Wiz, which published its own account on Wednesday. Wiz said it found the first flaw on 19 August "using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol", confirmed unauthenticated code execution against Drupal and WordPress within two days, and reported to PHP on 24 August. "Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit," it wrote, adding that the vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Wiz credited the PHP team, the security firm Calif and OpenAI for work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. Wiz's claim that PHP runs 70 per cent of websites is its own.
It was a crowded day. TechCrunch reported that Node.js patched four high-severity flaws, one allowing remote code execution, and that the LiteLLM proxy project said an attacker had published malicious packages to PyPI, Docker Hub and GitHub's container registry.
Why it matters: a pre-authentication code-execution bug in the language beneath a large share of the web, with no configuration that fully closes it, leaves patching as the only control. Wiz's timeline also shows how far AI tools compress the work: one day, by its account, from the first bug to a working exploit against Drupal. As we reported on Wednesday, eight certificate authority keys were the week's other infrastructure scare, and Railway has told every customer to rotate its keys.
